title: How To Begin Each Day On The Right Classroom Management Foot classroom-management-foot/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a step-by-step system for turning the first ten minutes of the school day into a tightly modeled, rehearsed procedure rather than leaving it to chance. His method includes modeling the correct entry routine as if he were a student, deliberately modeling the wrong way (a "how-not" strategy), having a student demonstrate the procedure for classmates, practicing it outside the classroom with backpacks on, repeating it a second time regardless of quality, and using a "do-it-again" strategy whenever the routine isn't done correctly. He also recommends lining students up outside before entry and greeting them there rather than inside, so the classroom itself becomes associated only with doing things right. The payoff, he argues, is a calmer, more independent, and more focused start to every school day.
points: The first few minutes of the school day set the behavioral tone for everything that follows and shouldn't be left to hope.
A "how-not" modeling strategy - deliberately demonstrating unwanted behaviors - sharpens students' understanding of expectations.
Practicing the entry procedure outside the classroom, then repeating and correcting it, cements the routine before it's needed for real.
Lining up and greeting students outside the room keeps the classroom itself associated only with doing things correctly.
A well-modeled opening routine reduces dependence on the teacher and channels students toward their own responsibilities.
quotes: Can you tell if you’re going to have a long behavior day within the first few minutes of the morning bell? Most teachers can.
The first few minutes of the school day set the behavioral tone for the rest of it. It’s not something you want to cross your fingers over.
Model your opening procedure as if you’re a student. Start outside your classroom–with backpack on–and walk through the entire routine as your students follow closely behind.
Now show your student how not to come in the classroom. Think of the behaviors you’ve seen from your students that you don’t want—and model them.
Watching a classmate successfully complete the procedure cements learning and eliminates excuses for not doing it correctly.

If your class doesn’t typically line up outside your room before school, I recommend you require them to. By having your students come in together, you can more easily associate the inside of your classroom with doing things the right way.
Starting each day with a detailed procedure is a simple way to ensure your students are ready for learning.
